nameStory: Rose Pogonia gets its name from its delicate pink flowers that resemble tiny roses perched on slender stems. The name 'pogonia' comes from the Greek word for 'beard,' referring to the fuzzy, hair-like projections on the flower's lip that look like a little yellow beard. It's also called 'snakemouth orchid' because the flower's shape resembles a snake's open mouth.
description: Rose Pogonia is a small, elegant wild orchid that stands 6-15 inches tall on a single slender stem. Each plant produces just one fragrant pink flower that sits above a single oval leaf partway up the stem. This delicate native orchid emerges from wet, boggy areas in late spring and early summer, creating magical moments for those lucky enough to spot one. Despite being an orchid, it's surprisingly hardy and can form small colonies in the right conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single pink flower with five petals and sepals surrounding a distinctive bearded lip marked with yellow and magenta streaks. The flower is sweetly fragrant and about 1 inch across.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: One oval leaf positioned about halfway up the stem, with parallel veins typical of orchids. The leaf feels smooth and somewhat waxy to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single unbranched stem rising 6-15 inches from boggy ground, with the flower held well above the solitary leaf like a pink beacon.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Develops a small capsule after flowering that splits open to release thousands of dust-like seeds that float on the wind.

habitat: Rose Pogonia thrives in wet, acidic habitats like sphagnum bogs, wet meadows, and the edges of marshes and ponds. Look for it in sunny to partially shaded areas where the soil stays consistently moist, often growing alongside sedges, wild cranberries, and other bog plants. It's scattered throughout New England but most common in areas with undisturbed wetlands.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge in late spring with the single leaf appearing first, followed by the distinctive pink flower bud developing at the stem tip.
seasonality.summer: Blooms peak in June and July, with the fragrant pink flowers lasting about two weeks. After blooming, small seed capsules begin to form.
seasonality.fall: Plants turn yellow and die back to underground roots, leaving small brown seed capsules that may persist into early fall before opening.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant underground with no visible parts above ground. Plants survive as small underground tubers until next growing season.

funFact: Rose Pogonia flowers are designed to fool bees! They offer no nectar reward but mimic other pink flowers that do, tricking hungry bees into visiting and accidentally picking up pollen packets that stick to their heads like tiny yellow crowns.
confusionNotes: The single pink flower and bog habitat make Rose Pogonia fairly distinctive, but it might be confused with Grass Pink orchid, which blooms in similar habitats. Remember: Rose Pogonia has one leaf halfway up the stem and flowers that face sideways, while Grass Pink has grass-like leaves at the base and flowers that face upward.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that New England has dozens of native wild orchid species beyond the showy tropical ones sold in stores. Rose Pogonia represents the subtle beauty of our native orchids and serves as an indicator of healthy wetland ecosystems that are increasingly rare.
compareHints: Rose Pogonia is the only species in its genus found in North America, making it unique among our native orchids. Compared to other small pink bog orchids like Grass Pink, Rose Pogonia is distinguished by its single mid-stem leaf, sideways-facing flowers, and the distinctive bearded lip with yellow markings. While Grass Pink has multiple grass-like leaves clustered at the base, Rose Pogonia's single leaf halfway up the stem is unmistakable.
